files.notes/close_checklist.md:
# June 2026 close — controller checklist

Owner: N. Vartanian. Complete in sequence; no shortcuts.

1. Reconcile operating cash to the June bank statement. For every book-side item identified, prepare one correcting journal entry per item.
2. Review the payroll register for any pay period ending after 6/30 and paying in July. If present, accrue the full gross wages to Accrued Liabilities; some months all runs pay in-month.
3. Confirm June prepaid amortization against the prepaid schedule and underlying contracts. Check the GL first to avoid duplication. If it is missing, book June amortization as ONE combined journal entry. Apply the convention that a full month is taken in the month each prepaid item begins.
4. Book June depreciation per the fixed asset register, after confirming the entry is not already in the GL.
5. Compare June vendor-bill documents with GL expense coding. Reclass anything miscoded to the correct expense account.
6. Prepare June budget-vs-actual variance commentary on an as-closed basis, after obligations 1-5 have been booked.
files.notes/company_background.md:
# Company background

Saltbox Mercantile Co. began in 2018 when two former retail buyers started assembling practical gift boxes from a shared studio near the waterfront. Their original idea was simple: make useful, design-conscious goods easier to discover without turning every purchase into a luxury occasion. The first assortment mixed pantry staples, desk accessories, small homewares, and paper goods from independent makers.

The business has since grown into a compact ecommerce operation serving individual shoppers, workplace teams, and a handful of wholesale customers. Its catalog still leans toward thoughtful everyday merchandise—kitchen tools, storage pieces, stationery, care packages, and seasonal collections—with an emphasis on items that ship well and feel personal on arrival.

The team is small and pleasantly opinionated. Merchandising debates happen beside packing tables, customer-service notes regularly shape product decisions, and operations staff are known to test new packaging with almost scientific seriousness. Marketing favors warm editorial photography and plainspoken product copy over hard-sell promotion.

Saltbox Mercantile Co. is currently focused on tightening its product mix, improving fulfillment routines, and building steadier relationships with makers and business customers. Leadership is also refining internal reporting so purchasing, campaign planning, and inventory decisions can be made with clearer information as the company continues its ordinary course of business.
files.notes/marketing_plan_h2.md:
# H2 marketing plan — working draft

## Direction
Give Saltbox Mercantile Co. a warmer, more consistent visual voice while keeping the practical, unfussy tone customers recognize.

## Priorities
- Roll out the brand refresh across the storefront, email templates, packaging inserts, and social profiles.
- Host two educational webinars per quarter, centered on gifting, workspace organization, and buying from independent makers.
- Test a partner co-marketing pilot with a complementary maker or workplace-services brand.
- Build seasonal editorial stories that connect products by use rather than by category alone.
- Improve post-purchase messaging with care tips, maker stories, and sensible cross-sell recommendations.

## Quarter focus
**Q3:** Finish creative standards, update core channels, recruit pilot partners, and establish webinar production routines.

**Q4:** Launch seasonal campaigns, expand the strongest partner concept, and reuse webinar material across email and social content.

## Measures to watch
Track qualified traffic, email engagement, repeat purchasing, webinar attendance, partner-sourced visits, and conversion by campaign theme. Keep reporting concise and separate durable gains from short promotional spikes.

Budget remains pending completion of the Q2 close.

# A few handoff notes

N. Vartanian—these are the items I would keep on the radar during close:

- The bank's own service fees and charges usually appear near the end of the statement. They have historically been picked up and booked during the close.
- Please look closely at June vendor-bill expense coding. A couple of items may be sitting in the wrong accounts, and the documents in `bills/` are authoritative if the GL description disagrees.
- The budget was fixed early in Q2. The one-off June items were not planned, so they should explain most of the larger budget-to-actual variances.
- Payroll timing is unusual this time: the second June run pays in early July. Confirm it against the payroll register.
